chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub from Aban ibn Taghlib said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who manumitted his female slave conditionally (dabbartu), then married her to another man, and she bore children from him. Then her husband died and left children from her. He said: 'Her children are like her status.' So when the one who manumitted her mother dies, they are free. I said to him: 'Is it permissible for the one who manumitted her mother to revoke the manumission if he needs to?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'What if you see that her mother dies after the husband has died, and her children from the free husband remain? Is it permissible for her master to sell her children and reclaim the manumission regarding them?' He said: 'No. He only has the right to reclaim the manumission regarding her mother if he needs to and she consents to that.'

key_terms.أُمّهُم: Their mother (referring to the slave woman).
key_terms.دَبّرَ: To conditionally manumit a slave, making them free upon the master's death or a specified event.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on revoking the manumission of a mudabbara slave woman and her children?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfabar elucidates the nuanced rules of 'tadbir' (conditional manumission) in Shia jurisprudence, specifically addressing the revocability of the mother's status versus the irrevocability of the children's status once the father is free. It highlights the scholarly distinction that while the master may reclaim the mother's servitude upon her consent if he has need, the children born to her from a free husband remain permanently free, illustrating the principle that the children's status is derived from the mother's condition at the time of birth but becomes independent upon her death. This ruling underscores the protective legal mechanisms for offspring in mixed-status unions within the Imami tradition.
